speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Defence. Last Thursday the Minister appeared to be quite confused in answering a question about the tragic loss of two planes and two pilots at Cold Lake. I trust by now the Minister's staff has briefed him and he can answer today in a more cogent manner. speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Solicitor General who, during the past two weeks, has refused to give a full account of the Hambleton affair and has left many contradictions in his answers. I have a specific question for the Solicitor General. We know that after April 25, 1980, Hambleton made aware to the Security Service the fact that he, Hambleton, was passing NATO secrets on to the Soviets. The Solicitor General has indicated to this House, and has indicated outside of the House, that no deal was made, that there was no promise of immunity. If that is, in fact, the case, could the Solicitor General tell us why did the Security Service never return to the Department of Justice with the necessary evidence there would have been in order to initiate a prosecution?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF RECOVERY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. As the Minister knows, increased capital spending is a key element in any recovery program. The forecasts now made by Industry,
December 13, 1982

Trade and Commerce show that new investment by large corporations will decline by $2.4 billion next year, an even larger drop than we experienced in 1982. Given the fact that these forecasts point to a potential loss of hundreds of thousands of jobs in 1983, will the Minister agree that we have now arrived at virtually a crisis situation, and will he bring in some kind of massive recovery program before the Christmas recess?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF RECOVERY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think that one very helpful first step in that regard will be for the House to pass the amendments to the Income Tax Act coming before the House this afternoon. This particular Bill provides for significant reductions in terms of individual and corporate tax. It would provide certainty in the business sector and would be quite helpful in ensuring that the private sector would know under what circumstances it will be operating in the next few months.
As far as the specific figures that the Hon. Member has referred to are concerned, he knows that these forecasts are only for the larger businesses. We are confident that the small business sector will see a turn-around. As the Hon. Member knows as well, the housing sector is certainly showing greater strength at the present time.

Madam Speaker,
I suspect that when we look closely at the amendments to the Income Tax Act we will actually see a loss of jobs as a result of that legislation, as opposed to anything additional.
The Minister must admit that another year of decline in corporate investment will not only mean that unemployed people will not go back to work but those who are already working will likely lose their jobs in the realm of hundreds of thousands in 1983. Does the Minister have any idea of how many jobs we will see lost in 1983?

Madam Speaker, I have indicated that the level of unemployment in 1983 would remain high but that it would gradually decline below 12 per cent before the end of the year. That is a situation that would be similar to the one that is being forecast in the United States and in most industrialized countries over the course of the next year. We plan to do everything that we can to bring that level of unemployment down as fast as possible. Obviously we have to do it in terms of an international environment that would be favourable, while using all the resources of the provincial and federal Governments to stimulate the economy over the next year.

It stopped the frantic rush by everyone to get a maximum catch from a common quota in a very short time, which had created problems in processing, marketing, quality control, and had resulted in inefficient use of boats, manpower and working capital. subtopic: REQUEST THAT PARLIAMENT BE CONSULTED ON POLICY
REQUEST THAT PARLIAMENT BE CONSULTED ON POLICY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the House knows that in January of this year, nearly a year ago, a Cabinet committee was going to implement a plan to salvage the Atlantic fisheries. They could not decide what to do, and so Mr. Kirby was appointed. He was going to report in July, then in September, then in November, and now possibly in January.
In view of the fact that the Minister of Veterans Affairs, a member of the Cabinet, has said that implementation of the Kirby Report would cost the taxpayers $100 million, and recent press reports quoting a source said that the bail-out is up to one-half a billion in debts and half as much again in working capital requirements, and the same source says that the ad hoc Cabinet committee is split, and in view of the almost incredible delay facing a fishery which everyone knows is in trouble, and knew it since the summer of 1981, when is the Minister going to present any policy for Atlantic Canada, and will Parliament have any say in it before it becomes policy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre De Bane (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
subtopic: REQUEST THAT PARLIAMENT BE CONSULTED ON POLICY

subtopic: CIRCUMSTANCES UNDER WHICH PROFESSOR WAS QUESTIONED
CIRCUMSTANCES UNDER WHICH PROFESSOR WAS QUESTIONED
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Solicitor General. After April 25, 1980, Mr. Hambleton gave a great deal of information to the RCMP security branch. Why did the Solicitor General not return to the Attorney General to obtain a legal opinion as to whether Mr. Hambleton should have been prosecuted at that time? Second, why did the Minister not ask for a legal opinion from the Attorney General on whether the circumstances under which Mr. Hambleton gave this information constituted an inducement?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bob Kaplan (Solicitor General of Canada):
subtopic: CIRCUMSTANCES UNDER WHICH PROFESSOR WAS QUESTIONED
speechtext: Madam Speaker, as I have indicated, the ground rules that were established for further questioning of Hambleton were that he would not be cautioned because, when he had been cautioned in the past, he had refused to give information about his role with NATO; that he would not be cautioned but that his cooperation would be sought. It was sought. It was forthcoming. Valuable information was obtained from him about NATO, but no third-party information was ever obtained by the Security Service, although it was agreed that, if further third-party information had been obtained, they would have indeed returned to the Attorney General of Canada and once again sought his consent.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
So we are
clear on the elements of the deal, is the Solicitor General saying that, on his side of the deal, the Government of Canada said that Hambleton would not be cautioned, and on Hamble-ton's side of the deal he said in exchange for that undertaking he would provide information? Are those the fundamental elements of the deal?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bob Kaplan (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there was no deal, as I have indicated everytime I have been asked that question. Hambleton gave his information because he was encouraged to do so. He was aware, 1 am sure, that without a caution that information would not be admissible. But the reason it was not admissible was not because of any agreement with him. It was not admissible because of my understanding and because of the advice we have had about the implications of the law.

subtopic: BRITISH DETECTIVES' WISH TO HAVE PROFESSOR RETURN TO CANADA

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: BRITISH DETECTIVES' WISH TO HAVE PROFESSOR RETURN TO CANADA
speechtext:
To coin a phrase, I find the Solicitor General incredibly naive. He tells us that in exchange for the undertaking that there would not be a caution, Hambleton gave information, but that was not a deal. Well, it is a deal in any other man's language, and I do not know why the Solicitor General will not admit in the House of Commons that he made a deal, and then, having done that, why he will not tell the House of Commons and the people of Canada what the consequences to Canada were of his deal.
Let me come to the question of the British. The Solicitor General earlier in this House today said he knew why British detectives tried to urge Hambleton to come back to Canada. He knew, but he will not tell Parliament. That is what he said. Will the Solicitor General tell us whether the immunity which Canada had granted Hambleton influenced the British detectives' decision to send him back to Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bob Kaplan (Solicitor General of Canada):
subtopic: BRITISH DETECTIVES' WISH TO HAVE PROFESSOR RETURN TO CANADA
speechtext: Madam Speaker, Canada did not give an immunity to Hambleton. I have indicated repeatedly that it was very clear to officials on our side, in Justice and in the RCMP, that if any basis could be found for prosecuting Hambleton after April 25, they would seek to do so. That is why I cannot understand how the Opposition can characterize that as a deal. The Government did not agree to give up anything to Hambleton in return for getting information, and Hambleton gave his information to them without any expectation that he would be any better off or any worse off for giving information. Therefore, there was not a deal within that very simple definition. There was no consideration coming from the Government, and there was no consideration expected by Hambleton.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
If the
Government of Canada did not give up the right to prosecute Hambleton, why did they not prosecute him?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bob Kaplan (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
The
Government of Canada did not prosecute Hambleton because no additional third-party evidence was forthcoming after April 25. They got a considerable amount of information of value. They shared that information with the Government of the United Kingdom and other friendly intelligence services, but it was not information which would have been admissible in a court in Canada, in the opinion of the law officers of the Crown, by the ground rules which they had set out in the meeting at which the decision of April was reached.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, a very brief supplementary. Was the arrangement his officials had with Hambleton-I will not call it a "deal" if the Minister insists-that no prosecution would be brought by the
Government of Canada except on the basis of third-party evidence?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bob Kaplan (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, we are learning the extent of the ignorance of the Leader of the Opposition of the law. It was not an agreement at all.
He is way ahead of you.

It was the effect of obtaining information from Mr. Hambleton without caution, and it was obtained from him without caution because efforts over a period of months to obtain information from him about NATO after caution had been unsuccessful. If the RCMP had been able to get his NATO connection from him before going to the Attorney General, they would have presented it to the Attorney General. They were unable to get it from him because he refused to answer questions relating to his role in NATO. After the meeting of April, 1980, the RCMP went back to Hambleton and told him of the decision which had been reached by the Attorney General. They asked for his co-operation, and Hambleton established a relationship with them which produced that information, and very good value was made of it, as the Hon. Member knows.

speechtext:

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Finance) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-139, an Act to amend the statute law relating to income tax (No. 2), be read the second time and referred to a Committee of the Whole.
He said: Madam Speaker, I am indeed very pleased to open the debate on this major Bill to amend the Income Tax Act. 1 want to discuss its provisions in both broad and specific terms. Not only is this legislation of great importance because of the positive changes it proposes in the tax system, but its passage will end the uncertainty that has lingered for too long on this subject. The Bill also provides an important example of the expanding role of consultation in shaping a tax system that works better for all of us.
As you know, the measures before us today represent the culmination of a process begun with the November, 1981 budget, the June, 1982 budget and my economic statement to
December 13, 1982

the House on October 27 this year. Since becoming Minister of Finance three months ago, I have looked forward to the day when we could get on with this final stage of the job. The time span covered by the process reflects the intensive and comprehensive consultation that has been followed.
My predecessor and I met directly with a wide range of individuals and organizations who had advice to give on tax issues. Members of the House and of the Senate have contributed greatly to the process through both formal and informal consideration of many of the issues. The Finance Committee of the House worked through the summer and reported in October. The Senate Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce also held hearings on the original ways and means motion. The Lortie Committee of outside experts has made a valuable contribution on the questions of inflation and taxation of personal investment income. Several other groups of outside tax experts and private sector representatives were appointed to examine important tax proposals.
The proof that all that consultation was for real is in the Bill itself. We asked for a lot of advice and we received it. More to the point, we accepted a lot of that advice and I will discuss some of those adjustments in just a few minutes.
We will continue to work to improve the consultative process in order to make the tax system more effective in achieving many important goals. We want to make the process more accessible to taxpayers. You will note, for example, that we have made available for the first time explanatory notes on the measures contained in the Bill. Those notes are written in a language that the average taxpayer can understand when he finds that a particular tax provision applies to him.
We have also made available draft regulations relating to the taxation of life insurance policies and annuity contracts. This is an area of particular complexity. By broadening the base on which budget decisions are made, we can look forward to both an improved process and improved results.
With this Bill today we are proposing commonsense management of the tax system. We have taken account of both the difficult current economic circumstances and the need to encourage a more efficient and productive economy through a tax system that is fair to taxpayers.
To accomplish those goals we must give immediate priority to creating a stable tax environment. Accordingly, the measures before us today reflect a number of decisions to delay or modify initiatives which, however worthy in their own right, would have created unwarranted disruption in a particularly difficult period for the economy.
As 1 have noted, there has been a lot of public debate about the Bill. Some of it has been highly emotional. It is understandable that particular groups and individuals should object strenuously to tax changes affecting them, and obviously it is understandable that people do not like to pay taxes. There is nothing new about this in the history of the world.
Income Tax
1 believe that Canadians as a whole understand that their Government cannot continue to spend more and more while it taxes them less and less. Equally they understand that taxes cannot be lowered for some without being raised for others. It is the job of the Minister of Finance, of the Government and of Parliament to weigh the merits of this or that special interest against the good of society as a whole.
Therefore, before getting down to specifics, 1 believe it would be extremely worthwile to look beyond the merits or acceptability of individual measures to specific interest groups and to focus on the fundamental thrust of this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, this Bill is based on the principle that the Canadian tax system is better off with lower tax rates applied to a broader income base. I firmly support this principle and 1 think it would be difficult to disprove it. Although many changes have been made to the Bill during the last few months, that same principle continues to be reflected in the tenor of the legislation before the House today, namely, that we should try to broaden the tax base and thus reduce tax levels. Actually, a tax system that rests on a broad base and provides for lower taxation rates is not superior in itself, but it is less likely to disrupt the market, to discourage individuals from saving, working and investing, in short, less likely to interfere with market operations and the rational allocation of resources.
We have heard a great deal about incentives. The basic incentives of our economic system are those created by the market, not by the tax system. The notion that a good dose of incentives would create a streamlined, flourishing and highly productive economy is simply unacceptable, since it would very probably lead to the creation of a motley group of overlapping and contradictory preferential measures.
I shall, if I may, clarify my position on this issue. 1 am not proposing, and I am not in favour of, a system totally devoid of tax incentives. In fact, even if we tried to achieve this, we would still have a system that would contain a certain number of incentives. A glance at the tax laws of almost any industrialized country in the world shows us that there are always a certain number of incentives in certain specific sectors. Some people think, and they are wrong, that the Government is trying to get rid of these incentives. 1 hasten to say that this is absolutely untrue and has no basis in fact. Even with the amendments we are proposing today, many incentives still remain in our tax legislation, and in fact, this Bill puts greater emphasis on some of those incentives. In fact, it has the advantage of reinforcing the impact of the remaining incentives and making them more effective. The proliferation of incentives in our tax system has unfortunately added to the daunting complexity of the system itself, and has aroused considerable criticism during the past few years.
I think the system should be further simplified, although we must not forget that it will necessarily reflect the complexity of

December 13, 1982
Income Tax
the world we live in. Furthermore, our desire to stabilize the tax environment unavoidably leads to some degree of complexity, which is evident in the wording of the legislation itself. Insofar as incentives continue to be a part of the system, they will continue to render it more complex. Nowhere has this been as obvious, perhaps, as in the small business sector. Year after year, Finance Ministers have received representations aimed at improving the tax system as it applies to small businesses in Canada, and year after year, they have proposed adjustments to that same tax system. The net result is, that today, we have a tax system for small businesses that is terrifying in its complexity, and that we shall now have to renew our efforts to take a less complex approach to small business taxation.

In effect, efforts have been made to simplify the Bill before the House today. The revised small business dividend tax measure about which I will speak in a moment is a good example. Moreover, I invited the Canadian Tax Foundation to suggest alternative approaches to tax simplification, with particular concentration on the issue of the taxation of small business. I am happy to report that the Canadian Tax Foundation accepted my invitation and that it is preparing itself to work on the very issue in the next few months. It may well be impossible to make major headway in simplifying the tax law until we are again prepared to address the issue of eliminating more special provisions, broadening the tax base, and reducing tax rates.
For example, much, if not all, of the complexity in the small business tax system arises because of the special tax rate which provides over $1.2 billion a year to small businesses and is being enriched in this Bill. The fact is that the small business tax system would be much simpler if tax rates were the same as those for other corporations, just as unincorporated small businesses are taxed like other individual taxpayers. I am not suggesting that incentives to small businesses are a bad thing, and I doubt if anyone would suggest it, but it underlines the point that tax complexity is one of the prices to be paid for special treatment of any group.
Before dealing with some of the specific measures and adjustments in the Bill, permit me a further word on the subject of consultation. Some people have interpreted the Government's response to the consultation process as a sign of weakness. Some have catalogued the number of changes made as a result of the process and interpreted it as a sign that the whole Bill should or would be withdrawn. With all due respect,
I say that this is irresponsible. I suppose it is the old game in politics of being damned if you do and damned if you don't.
If you have a bad Bill, you withdraw it.

The Government's responsiveness is a sign of its commitment to consultation and of its repectiveness to constructive comment. I will illustrate that point by citing the
Government's response to particular issues raised by the House committee and many other groups and individuals. My colleague, the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove), will address in detail the consultation and response that has been made on the taxation of life insurance. I would like to thank my colleague and many of our backbenchers for their contribution in the analysis of this very complex and very difficult issue. I would like to express my appreciation to them for the excellent work which they have done in bringing before the House measures that I think meet most, if not all, the objections raised to previous proposals. I would merely cite this area of life insurance as evidence that significant adjustments can be made while preserving the basic intent of broadening the tax base in a fundamentally fair and efficient manner.
Another example. The November budget imposed a tax on dividend distributions by small business with a very specific and defensible purpose. The aim is to ensure that income withdrawn from a small busines for personal use of owners is taxed in the same way as other income, including hard-earned wages and salaries.
That is nonsense.
Few have disputed the basic purpose of this tax.
Oh, oh!
Come on, thousands have.

You see another example across the aisle of people who are criticizing before hearing it all, Mr. Speaker. The measure was criticized for its complexity and also for its application to dividends paid out of income earned before the measure was introduced.
You withdrew it.

That is right. I am glad to hear that. What we have done is to take account of those criticisms and representations. That issue was raised by several organizations: for instance, the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants; the Canadian Bar Association; the Canadian Federation of Independent Business; the CMA; the Tourism Industry Association of Canada.
Why didn't you forget about it then?

I invite my hon. friend to read at least the explanatory notes if he cannot read the Bill. He will find that we have taken into account those representations and amended the Bill. The Bill before us today does address those very concerns. The tax applies only to dividends paid out of income earned after 1982. We are not taxing dividends that have been accumulated in the past. This and other technical adjustments have allowed for significant simplification of these rules. This is a very important example of how the process of consultation can be carried on effectively and how we can end up with a better system, one less complex but which will at the same time be fairer to the average taxpayer. It will make the
December 13, 1982

Canadian taxpayer, whether he is taking his money in the form of dividends or whether he is getting it in the form of wages and salaries, feel that he is being treated equitably and fairly and that there is no undue advantage to one taxpayer because he happens to get his money in one form rather than in another form.
Another area that raised concern was the question of the liability of a director of a company. This was addressed in the November, 1981 budget. That budget proposed to expand the liability of a director by imposing joint and several liability on directors where the corporation fails to withhold various payroll and non-resident taxes. The House Finance Committee noted that the Canadian Bar Association considered the scope of the application too broad. Similar representations were made by other groups. In response, we have amended the proposal to include a due care and diligence test to ensure that innocent directors are not adversely affected in cases where taxes are withheld but not remitted.
In response to advice from the Finance Committee of this House and various professional associations, the change in treatment of professionals' work in progress will not apply to professionals who are ineligible for the low small-business tax rate or who would be ineligible if they were incorporated. This includes doctors, dentists, lawyers, accountants, veterinarians and chiropractors, among others, and will mean that many professionals will not have to face the complexity and the paper burden represented by evaluating every file which they have on record at the end of every year. That measure has been abandoned, and this decision, I would argue, has been very well received by all parties concerned.
It was stupid in the first place.

Although not part of this legislation, I would like to say a word about the proposed move of the federal sales tax from the manufacturers' to the wholesale level. This is an issue of importance for both small and large business. In response to representations, the introduction of this measure is being delayed. This will provide time for further consultation with industry representatives who suggest that a modified proposal might achieve our objectives of improving the tax structure and removing some serious biases in favour of imported goods over those manufactured in Canada. 1 have invited interested associations to designate their representatives, and I expect to be able to announce the composition of that task force in the next few days. We will see this further phase of consultation going ahead soon. Again, what is required is rational debate and rational and thorough examination of an issue that is very complex.
My colleagues in this House will no doubt have read press reports put out by business groups who have complained that we have not proceeded with this measure aimed at transferring the federal sales tax from the manufacturers' level to the wholesale level. On the other hand, I and Members of this House have been receiving many representations from other business groups saying "Don't do a thing; don't proceed with this now".
Income Tax
In effect, we have a strong division of views among the business community in this regard. We have sectors, such as the auto parts industry in particular, which claim that the present regime favours imports at the expense of domestically produced parts. Also we have a number of businesses, retail and wholesale, that say they cannot afford to assume an additional burden at the present time, that there must be a better way. So we agreed to give them some time. As a matter of fact, 1 have indicated that we would give them until at least the middle of 1984, the next 18 months, to sit down in an attempt to work out between themselves as well as with the Government a better way of doing it.
One fact which must be made clear is that we will not be able to continue indefinitely with the present arrangement. Clearly, I am sure any Party in the House would not want to encourage this direction of favouring imports rather than Canadian production in certain sectors in particular. Instead of telling the Government to abandon its notion of taxation at the wholesale level, we must all try to find a better solution than what is in place at the present time. I recognize that this is not a particularly easy task since it is a complex problem which implies changing some of the traditional, well-established practices of many businesses. Some of these businesses have been doing well with the present regime by avoiding some requirements that they may be faced with under a different regime.
Again, the House will be invited in due course, after those consultations have taken place, to consider a changed system, which 1 hope will carry broad support because I do not think there is much disagreement over the fundamental objectives being pursued in these particular amendments.
To underline the Government's commitment to consultation and stability in the tax system, I have also made clear again that the proposal will not be implemented before the legislation on wholesale tax receives Royal Assent after being passed through both Houses of Parliament.
The consultation process has also led to significant adjustments in proposals affecting the taxation of personal investment incomes. The proposed restriction of deductibility for interest expense has been dropped on the advice of a committee of prominent tax professionals. We will also be proceeding with draft legislation for a registered shareholder investment plan under which the taxation of capital gains will be limited to the real after inflation gain. The Lortie Committee, to which I have referred already and which endorsed such a plan as proposed by my predecessor, has also proposed a major study of the desirability of adjusting the taxation of business income for inflation. We hope to proceed in that direction shortly. This will clearly be an important area of exploration in the continuing effort to improve the tax system in an orderly, consultative manner.
I have already noted that the Government remains committed to special measures to assist small business in spite of the associated problem of tax complexity. This support of small

December 13, 1982
Income Tax
business is one goal that this Government has always been committed to. Today, 1 would like to give a very clear renewed commitment to this support, and since my appointment 1 have made it a point of consulting quite frequently and regularly with the official spokesmen representing various areas of small business in this country.
A very significant example of the commitment of this Government to help small business is provided in this Bill. The amount of income subject to the low small-business tax rate is being raised from $150,000 to $200,000 annually and from $750,000 to $1 million in total retail earnings. These measures should be of substantial help to the Canadian small business sector at the present time.
As Members know, in the case of manufacturing profits the tax rate for small business corporations is 10 per cent as compared to 30 per cent for larger corporations. For other types of active business income, the small business rate is 15 per cent instead of 36 per cent for larger corporations. Therefore, the benefit is clearly in substantial favour of small business in this country. This Bill provides significant new incentive for the growth of the small business sector in Canada.
This Bill also gives effect to an extension of the Small Business Bond to assist eligible small businesses in financial difficulty. This is a measure which I announced in October.

Measures affecting all taxpayers included a proposal to tax benefits derived from private health insurance and dental care plans. This proposal would have made the tax system more equitable, but representations against the proposal were made before the House Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, by many groups, including the Life Underwriters Association of Canada, the Canadian Life and Health Insurance Association, the Canadian Manufacturers Association, the Canadian Federation of Labour, the Canadian Association of University Teachers, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business and the Canadian Dental Association.
I concluded that the time was not ripe to introduce this measure. The benefits of the average health insurance and dental care plan for a married couple may total from $400 to $600 per year. Tax on these amounts would have been from $120 to $175 for the employee with an average income. Thanks to the decision announced in my statement in the House on October 27 of this year, Canadians will not have to pay this tax.

The result of abandoning this measure will be that the health and dental care insurance premiums or contributions paid by the employers will not be subject to taxation for the employee. This will be of significant help to those workers who are presently benefitting from health or dental care plans in their jobs. It is a significant tax relief which would not have been available had we proceeded with this particular measure.

The bill before the House today has also absorbed a number of important aspects of the 6 and 5 program, reflected in the capping of indexation of personal income tax rates at 6 and 5 per cent for the next two years. I am glad to see that in Canada, the rate of inflation is falling towards the 6 and 5 level. If we manage to control inflation, the impact of capped indexation on the Canadian taxpayer will be considerably lessened and even practically non-existent, if we reach our objective.
I think this measure aptly illustrates the validity of the 6 and 5 program, which, in fact, cancels out its own drawbacks in the short term, while providing the tremendous advantage of reducing inflation in the long term. We should also remember that since 1974, Canadians have had the benefit of full indexation of personal income tax. Furthermore, indexation at 6 and 5 is clearly preferable to the complete absence of indexation experienced by the American taxpayers over the same period, that is, since 1974. In fact, many Canadians are unaware that people in the United States do not have the indexation which Canadian taxpayers have enjoyed since 1974. Many Canadians pointed out to us that last year in the United States, they had a tax reduction of 10 per cent. What they forgot, however, is that since 1974, Americans had not enjoyed the tax rate indexation we had here in Canada, and that Canadians, as a result of the indexation since 1974, had enjoyed a far more substantial tax adjustment than the one announced last year by President Reagan and adopted by the U.S. Congress.
In addition to indexation at 6 and 5 per cent, this Bill provides for a general reduction in income tax starting in 1982 and totalling more than $1 billion per year. I may add that this measure has not received the attention it deserves. I cannot blame the Opposition, because that is not really their role. They are supposed to point out the negative aspects they see or think they see in any draft legislation introduced by the Government. Nevertheless, the Canadian taxpayer ought to know that the Bill before Parliament today will mean a general tax reduction of over $1 billion in 1982.
For a married worker with two dependent children and earning the average industrial wage of $22,000 per year, the reduction in tax rates and the reduction in Federal transferable tax will mean a savings of over $220 per year. Furthermore, the Child Tax Credit has been increased by $50 per year per child, up to a maximum of $343 for fiscal 1982. This measure will mean a savings of another $100 for low or middle-income families with two dependent children.
The Bill also provides for a reduction in Federal tax, so that the taxpayer with a dependent spouse and an income of less than $20,000 will save an additional $200.
The Opposition, especially the Members of the New Democratic Party, has tried, during the last few months or weeks, to convince us that the tax changes contained in this bill will only benefit people with income of $100,000 and over, in other
December 13, 1982

words, people in the upper tax bracket. However, the facts 1 mentioned earlier clearly demonstrate that millions of Canadians, and I say millions of Canadians will benefit from the tax advantages provided by the draft legislation being considered by Parliament today. I am not referring to Canadians in the upper tax bracket but to Canadians with incomes of less than $20,000 per year, and workers earning an average industrial wage of $22,000 per year, who will benefit substantially from the tax changes contained in the Bill before the House today. As 1 said before, the general reduction in income tax rates provided in this Bill should encourage Canadians to save and invest in order to develop our country. The Bill represents a substantial structural change in the system, and its long-term benefits are very promising. Nevertheless, we must not lose sight of our fiscal responsibility. Earlier, I commented that few people like to pay taxes. In fact, I think all Canadians would prefer their taxes to go down or disappear altogether. However, even in the best of worlds, taxes would be inevitable.
In these difficult times, the Government is under constant pressure from all sides to spend more money or to reduce taxes in order to stimulate the economy. Often, I see people who ask me to spend more money, reduce taxes and reduce the Government's deficit, all at the same time. I must admit that my officials and advisers and I have been unable to find a way to achieve all three objectives at the same time.
My hon. colleague, however, seems to have found a way to reduce taxes, expenditures and the deficit. I noticed that when his party was in power, it failed to find the magic formula, and 1 am afraid that any claims that one would be able to do all three simultaneously are more reminiscent of the claims of snake oil salesmen than of the principles of economics or sound fiscal management.
Why don't you let us take over, Marc, and then you'll find out?
The Hon. Member says that we should let them take over and we would find out. The Canadian public did find out in 1980, and after six months they could not stand it any more.
Now they wish we were back.

I would suggest to the Hon. Member that the recipe has not been tried and that the Canadian people rejected being force-fed the kind of economic horse medicine that the Conservative Party was trying to impose upon them.
[ Translation]
Notwithstanding interruptions by my colleagues opposite, I shall listen carefully to any suggestions and give them my attention. However, I urge Hon. Members to remember the economic problems facing our country and this Government at the present time with respect to our fiscal policy, as a result of the automatic impact the recession has on our tax system.
Income Tax
Government revenue has dropped considerably-by several billion dollars-because corporate profits are down, as well as personal income, and the latter particularly as a result of unemployment. Thus, Government revenue has fallen dramatically and at the same time, Government expenditures have increased very substantially, because we have to provide assistance to people who are hurt by the recession. We have had to help hundreds of thousands of Canadians who are now unemployed and are either drawing unemployment insurance benefits or welfare or being helped by one of the many direct employment programs created by the Government to help Canadians cope with the economic crisis we are going through at the present time. Financially, our room to manoeuvre has shrunk considerably. In the circumstances, it is impossible to grant further substantial tax breaks to any group without increasing taxes for another group in order to bring down Government expenditures by a corresponding amount. The bill before the House today, Mr. Speaker, reflects fiscal reality, because it proposes a balanced selection of carefully thought out measures aimed at improving the tax climate, laying the foundation for economic recovery and enabling Canadians- and this is very important-to continue to help those who need help.

In conclusion, I believe the basic philosophy of this Bill is sound.
What about the tax increases?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Iron-clad.
Its provisions are good and it responds to criticisms which have been made.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Here? Where?
The time has come to pass this legislation. The time has come to end the uncertainty surrounding these tax issues.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Never should have been started.

The time has come to move on and to face and solve the pressing and serious problems before us. The passage of this legislation is a prerequisite for further budgetary moves directed at our economic problems.
Don't hit us again.

It would be irresponsible to introduce a new budget before the uncertainty of the old measures is cleared up. I can say, in the process of consultations I have had since I have been appointed Minister of Finance, that this is the message that has been repeated over and over again to me by everybody I have consulted. This message has come through quite clearly from the 30 different organizations with whom I

December 13, 1982
Income Tax
have had meetings in the first month and a half after my appointment.
Why did you not bring the budget in then?
That message has been clearly repeated since 1 started consulting, anticipating the next budget.
Why the delay in bringing it in?
What message?
The Hon. Member is asking what is the message. The message is that we should pass the legislation resulting from the previous budgets-
Why did you wait two months to bring it in?

-that we should clear the air, that we should remove the uncertainty and that we should not proceed with a new budget until we at least know exactly what is happening with the measures resulting from the previous budgets. The message from labour, management, farming organizations and small business has been clear; they want to know what the rules of the game are going to be.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: You will change them anyway.

They want to be assured by Parliament that the measures affecting the fiscal situation for 1982 are going to be implemented without further delay and without leaving an air of uncertainty around those measures.
1 read last week that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) declared that he would do everything he could to block this legislation and prevent it from going ahead. Obviously, I can understand that in a flight of high rhetoric any politician can make high-sounding statements. 1 hope this is one of those. Obviously, the Opposition can drag out this Bill for a very extended period, but I believe that the Opposition will adopt a more responsible attitude and, after due consideration, we will be able to proceed not only with debating these measures but with the voting on and adoption of them. They have been the subject of extensive debate over the last year.
It is the first time they have hit the House.

They have been the subject of consideration by outside experts, by groups and organizations that have made representations before the Government, before parliamentary committees, the committee of the House and the committee of the Senate. The committee of the House sat through the summer right into the fall, heard briefs and made representations. How much more study do we need?
You are starting to weep now. Wipe the tear from your eye, Marc.

In fact, we know now exactly what kind of measures the Government is proceeding with. I have indicated the changes that have been made. A number of those changes have already been included in the Bill which was considered by
the parliamentary committee, and I submit to the House that the Canadian public is expecting us to proceed expeditiously-
And responsibly.

And responsibly-with this particular measure.
As far as we on this side of the House are concerned, we will co-operate to provide all the information that is relevant and required, but at the same time I hope that we get good cooperation from other Members of the House to make sure that this Bill receives Royal Assent with not too long a delay.
I remind the Members of this House that last year there were more than 15 million tax returns filed, of which more than 11 million resulted in refunds. We expect this year there will be even more refunds than last year because there are people who have been unemployed during the course of the year who will have a lower level of income than they had anticipated and will be entitled to significant and I hope large tax refunds when they file their income tax return.
Early passage of the legislation will help Revenue Canada get on with the job of processing the 1982 returns and mailing the refunds to Canadian citizens who are entitled to them. It is clear that many Canadians will be in urgent need of their tax refunds during the period we are going through. I therefore look forward to a speedy debate that recognizes the extensive consultation process that has contributed so much to the Bill before us.
My colleague, the Minister of State for Finance, will be taking this Bill through the House during the debate and consideration before committee.
No.

My Parliamentary Secretary and myself will be very happy to be present and to give him a hand whenever he needs a hand. 1 must say my colleague has shown such competence, such ability and such expertise in that subject-
When?

I started those consultations last week in Vancouver, for instance, with the B.C. Employers' Council and representatives of the labour movement. That organization will be able to present a formal brief to me within the next two or three weeks.

Mr. Speaker, today we are commencing the first formal consideration of the tax legislation arising out of the November budget, some 13
Income Tax
months after the fact. That is far too long a period of time for Canadians to wait. It is incredible that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) should be urging this House to move quickly on this legislation when we have just now seen the Bill representing that budget, plus the June budget, plus his October statement, all brought into one omnibus piece of tax legislation. The Government House Leader is urging us to come to grips with this Bill and pass it within the next eight sitting days. That is unacceptable.
Much has been lost since that time, 13 months of valuable time. A Minister has lost his job and a Deputy Minister has lost his job. A Government which used to pride itself on being known as a competent manager has lost all credibility as well as the confidence of the Canadian people.
More seriously, in human terms over 500,000 people have lost their jobs and some 50,000 bankruptcies have been declared during this period. To put this in some perspective, that over 500,000 job loss figure is just about equal to the entire population of Quebec City or Calgary, Edmonton, Winnipeg or Hamilton. It is an incredible figure.
Also during this period of time Canada has seen its place in the international community slip noticeably. We have seen articles in the London Economist entitled "Maple Leaf Crumbles", as well as in The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times and Business Week. These stories were not written in anger or with any vindictiveness but with sorrow and disbelief that we as a country have plunged so low in spite of our rich human and natural resources.
That November budget played a pivotal role in this decline. In my opening statement following the Minister's speech at the time of that budget, I warned of a tax revolt. Those words were acutely prophetic, judging from what in fact has happened since then.
Let me remind Hon. Members of the reaction to that budget. I want to direct these words to some of the Liberal Members. I quote from The Toronto Star of November 14 last year:
Liberal politicians were chuckling like schoolboys yesterday.
For the relaxing Liberals the snickering came at Wilson's expense.
"There is nothing he can say against this budget", said one smiling Liberal who has aspirations of a Cabinet post in next February's promised shuffle.
Maybe it was the Hon. Member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson) who made that snickering comment.
"We covered everything. There is just nothing left to criticize."
While many Liberals were in a buoyant mood yesterday, their glee could swiftly change to sorrow if MacEachen's objective of reducing inflation by cutting the deficit, withholding investment incentives and avoiding either a tax increase or reduction for average consumers backfires ... So while the bored Liberal backbenchers were able to giggle and laugh yesterday in the sleepy Commons, economic realities may come crashing down on them with each new release from Statistics Canada of inflation and unemployment rates as well as the Bank of Canada's weekly interest rate lottery.
I mention that because I want to remind Liberal Members how wrong they were. Thirteen months ago today they sat snickering on the other side of the House, thinking that that

1 wish to quote from a few reports and other representations that have been made to me and other Conservative Members about that budget. Mr. MacEachen's can of worms.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Economic Development; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: You are dealing with ancient history. Why don't you deal with the budget?

I am not dealing with ancient history, I am dealing with this tax legislation. Many of the same things that these people spoke of are still in this legislation. I will be coming back to that in due course, if the Member has any patience and can keep himself in the House and not snicker behind the curtain.
The next quote is from an older gentleman:
I was trying to save the Government from having to support me in my old age. Damn the Government now. I am going to spend every cent I can get my hands on and when I run out of money I won't be ashamed to ask the Government for help. They're certainly not ashamed of taking it from us.
And the next one:
The November 12th budget pulled the rug from under my feet. If that "Financial fiasco" is implemented, it appears that our family farm will no longer exist and my family will be forced to accept a lower standard of living.
The final quote I want to give, Mr. Speaker, is this:
We object to the victimization of low and middle income groups to trap the affluent.
All of these quotes came to me from real people. We received them in the course of our meetings across the country. There is no imagination here; these are real quotes. The Minister implied that we are using our imagination in drumming up criticism of this budget. These are real people assessing the true impact of that budget, this tax legislation, on their lives, on their jobs, their businesses and their families. Many of these statements have been confirmed by the experience of the past 13 months and are still very pertinent to this legislation.
Our Party opposed that budget right from the start. We encouraged the Government not to proceed without a full public debate. We wanted those most affected to be able to explain to the Government the true damage which the budget was going to cause. The Government refused this course of action, probably out of crass political self-interest, because as we look back over the past 13 months it is incredible the number of changes which have been made. There have been as many as 47 changes. Some areas have been changed a full three times. That is a clear indication that the Minister and his officials proceeded with this major tax reform in a totally blind vacuum. Many areas were changed, including multiple unit residential buildings, capital cost allowances, retiring allowances, work in progress, employee benefits, life insurance and annuities, automobile stand-by charges, charitable foundations, housing and travel benefits and Small Business Bonds. Most of these changes were only transitional in nature, and that is what brings us to this particular piece of legislation.
We called for a new budget and, Mr. Speaker, some people criticized us at the time for being too blatantly partisan; but
December 13, 1982

considering the piece of legislation which is before us today, how much better, how much less destructive, it would have been had the Government taken our advice and introduced a new budget. Instead, we have had an ongoing series of changes over the past 13 months. Changes have been made, I think, some six or seven different times during that 13-month period. The changes have been spread over that full year and the uncertainty of not knowing whether further changes would be made has hurt many small businesses, many business plans, and has contributed directly to the job loss we have suffered during this period. It is as if the budget has been struck as a flash fire strikes a building. Much of the interior is destroyed, but the building is still left standing.
Let us look at what is left in that budget, Mr. Speaker, the contents of the Bill before us, and try to judge whether the entire budget should have been scrapped back in November-December of last year. It is ironic, but the most damaging part of the budget will not even be voted upon by this House. The change in capital cost allowance, which has had the effect of reducing the amount of investment in new plant and equipment and other job-creating projects, will be dealt with by regulation. I ask Liberal Members of Parliament whether they are happy that this Government has slipped this one by them without even having had a chance to consider it in the House of Commons. Investment in new plant and equipment has dropped by 12 per cent in Canada over a one-year period.
The Canadian Manufacturers' Association says that manufacturers will not show any investment growth until 1985. The comparable figure in the United States is down 6 per cent. The reduction in the capital cost allowance clearly has been the major factor in the poor performance in Canada. It is also a clear reason why over the past year our unemployment rate has gone up four percentage points, while that in the United States has only gone up three percentage points. Our unemployment rate is standing now at 12.7 per cent, almost two percentage points higher than in the United States.
The areas which do remain from the budget and which are in this legislation will compound an already poor economy. The small businessman is hit particularly hard. The 12.5 per cent small business distribution tax remains. Deferred profitsharing plans are now almost totally impractical for all but a few small businesses. There will be a considerably less favourable treatment of a capital gain in the sale of a business where the payment stretches over a period of years. The gutting of the Small Business Development Bond and its replacement by the small business bail-out bond makes this type of financial support almost unavailable to small businesses.
Finally, an element which the Minister totally ignored in his remarks earlier is that the small business lower tax rate will be lost when the cumulative earnings of a company reach SI million, regardless of the amount of earnings retained in the business and regardless of the amount of capital needed to run that business. The result of this is that in time many small businesses will be taxed at the same tax rate as the largest businesses in Canada. The effect of this is to put the real risk-takers of the country on the same basis as the large companies
Income Tax
and the salaried employees, and that, Mr. Speaker, is a totally wrong way to go. Is it any wonder that the small business community is now almost totally opposed to the Liberal Party of Canada? Is it any wonder that they and other Canadians are very apprehensive about their future? The new Minister of Finance has said there will not be any further tax reform for now as long as we are in a recession. Small businessmen are terribly worried that, as soon as the economy turns around, the Liberals will spring the rest of the MacEachen budget without any warning. The changes in interest deductibility, the federal sales tax and the tighter rules on capital gains are three examples of what they are fearing right now.
The construction industry has been suffering terribly in the past year. It suffers from some of the same effects of this budget as the small businessman. The result is that thousands of workers have been laid off. Yet the Government persists in retaining the capital cost allowance changes and the new policy to capitalize so-called soft costs during construction. Previously, architects' and engineers' fees, legal fees, fees for interest costs during construction, could be charged against current income. Now they must be capitalized. The result of this is that these two changes remove a considerable amount of cash income at the start of a major capital investment. The consequence is that, with the very high interest rates today, many projects have become uneconomical. Many are cancelled, jobs are lost. This indicates that these changes are sheer madness at a time of high unemployment. Either that or the government displays a total ignorance of or insensitivity to the effect of the changes, which is massive job loss in that industry.
Forward averaging is another backward step in this legislation. It is being sold by the Minister and his Department as a fair means of spreading the tax load. But let us be honest with the taxpayer: it is a sneaky way of transferring money from the private sector to the public sector.
There has been a system of forward averaging in place for a number of years now. It was called an income averaging annuity contract, IAAC for short. IAACs allowed the taxpayer to spread over an extended period the tax load of a large bulge in taxable income-for instance, from the sale of a business or a farm. Now these options are much more restricted. There will be no more IAACs and no general averaging. The taxpayer either pays taxes on the large income in that year or he averages it over future years.
The Government has a number of assumptions on how this forward averaging works, and they can come up with some assumptions which show the income averaging annuity is about the same as forward averaging. This requires some very selective assumptions, but it does not work in most normal cases. Let us for a minute just accept the Government's assumptions and reasoning here. The big difference between the IAAC, on the one hand, and forward averaging, on the other hand, is that with an IAAC the money is left in the hands of the private sector. The taxpayer gives the money to his choice of trust company or insurance company to invest.

December 13, 1982
Income Tax
His money will be invested in real estate, mortgages, stock or bonds-creating jobs, generating income and more production.
With forward averaging, the new approach, the money goes to the Government, to the bureaucrat to invest, perhaps in Maislin or Dome. It will be invested not in productive job-creating projects, but probably in make-work programs.
This is an excellent example of the difference between the Conservative Party and Liberals and the NDP. We have opposed the loss of lAACs strongly. We believe the money will be more productive to the economy if left in the private sector. The other two parties want it left with the Government where it can be controlled by decision makers here in Ottawa. The result will be a less productive economy and more people out of work.
There is another reason that we oppose forward averaging. If a taxpayer elects forward averaging today, he must pay the taxes now at the top personal rate and take his chances that in the future he will recover some of these taxes if his rate in those future years is lower than the top rate. Who is likely to benefit from this system? The person in the top income bracket? Probably, because he has nothing to lose; either way he has to pay taxes at the top rate.
What about the person in a lower income bracket? He has a very difficult decision to make. If he elects forward averaging, he must pay taxes today at the top rate and hope he can get it back in future years if his taxes are lower. But if he guesses wrong, he will have paid more tax than he should to the Government. With forward averaging, he has to survive to get the benefits. With an 1AAC, his surviving wife and children receive the proceeds. With forward averaging, the agreement expires upon his death.
In effect, it is heads the Government wins, tails the taxpayer loses-except for the wealthy taxpayer, about whom the Liberals seem to be more concerned than the vast number of small businessmen and farmers who make up an important part of the vast group of middle income Canadians who have given this country such strength and stability over the years but have been so severely attacked by the budget and by this legislation.
Let me point out two other aspects of this Bill which run directly counter to the interests of the country.

Last week, the Government tabled its proposals on pension reform. The message of that report is clear: Canadians are not adequately prepared for retirement. And now, in this Bill, the Government is discouraging Canadians from saving through RRSP's or other plans. Who is going to be hurt most by this measure? Not the person who is well-off and can find various ways of reducing his taxable income. The impact of this measure will be felt most severely by those on low incomes, who probably do not have decent pension plans and who need interest deductibility most. To many of these people, a loan contracted at the end of February in order to be able to
contribute to an RRSP is a form of forced saving, and they will have to work very hard to pay off the loan in the following months. If there is any abuse among those in the upper tax brackets, by all means put a stop to it, but not if it means discouraging saving for one's retirement.

Mobility of Canadians has always been an important part of our work life. National companies have traditionally moved their staff around, giving them experience and exposing them to different parts of the country. Here again, the tax Bill takes a major step backward by taxing the benefit received on low-cost loans made to assist this type of move. The Government has said this is a loophole that the rich are taking advantage of, yet company after company has shown that these loans have been made more to their lower and middle management than top management people. There could not be a loophole for the rich because there is already a $50,000 limit on the size of loan allowed under the existing rules.
This is another example of how the middle income people in this country are being attacked by the Liberal Government. I hope that in Committee of the Whole and in subsequent speeches Members opposite and the Minister will tell us what they have against the middle income earners in our country.
We oppose the limitation of the indexation factor on personal taxes according to the six and five program. This is nothing more than a sneaky income tax increase. If the Government wishes to increase taxes, let it do so. To slip this through without proper debate and backed up by a massive advertising program supporting the six and five program is pure and simple deceit.
Now is not the time to increase taxes. The economy is still in decline. Canadians should be encouraged to spend their money. A tax increase to feed the ever-growing appetite of the Government is counter-productive.
If the Government feels so strongly about the size of the deficit, let it cut spending. Let it curtail the 50 per cent increase in ministerial travel. Let it keep its little JetStars on the ground. Let it cut back on the size of the increase in the Minister's Department and show it means business. Let it cut back where any businessman would start-on overhead and the administrative costs of running the Government. We have yet to hear why the overhead costs in the 12 largest Departments will increase by 17.1 per cent. These are not my figures; these are Government figures taken from the Blue Book of the Government Estimates this year. I say do not increase personal taxes; rather, reduce Government spending and get the Government off our backs.
There have been many changes to the original proposals on life insurance and annuities, as I have already indicated. The rules of the game have changed significantly. If a policy is cancelled because of a financial emergency, the tax consequences are major. The tax on surrender will increase by between 25 per cent and 50 per cent-depending on the age of the person-just when the policy holder can least afford it.
December 13, 1982

Policy loans-loans using the insurance policy as collateral-will now be taxed. This again will occur when the policy holder can afford it the least.
The conversion of an insurance policy into an annuity will be taxed on the same basis as if the policy were cancelled. Surely this ignores totally the use of life insurance as a source of retirement income after the policy holder reaches a certain age and his dependants no longer need life insurance protection.
This tax Bill also continues the unfair requirement to tax the interest element of deferred annuity contracts every three years, even though no cash income has been received. There may have been abuses here, but no recognition is being made of those annuities which are purchased for true retirement purposes.
Together these provisions attack retirement planning and run totally counter to the spirit of pension reform which this same Minister and his colleagues espoused last week. Words are cheap Mr. Speaker, but actions reveal far more accurately the philosophy and policy of this Government.
This tax Bill says one of two things, Mr. Speaker. Either the Government is not prepared to follow through with real actions to support the desire of Canadians to prepare for a happy, selfreliant retirement, or the Government is attempting to undermine this healthy motive in the hope that retiring Canadians will be thrown more into the hands of Government. This potential loss of freedom and independence for our retiring Canadians poses a serious question for all Members.
There is another part of this tax bill which is a bit of a sleeper. The Minister has never discussed it before. It has to do with the long-standing principle of confidentiality in the tax system. The legislation now requires information regarding the name, address, occupation or type of business of a taxpayer to be given to other federal or provincial Departments for the purpose of enabling these Departments to do analyses and research work. What does this mean? What information is required? How detailed will it be? How soon will it be before the specific tax information will be bandied about? What control will there be on how these other Departments use that information?
Also this amendment extends the access to tax information for purposes of administering the Petroleum Incentives Program and the Unemployment Insurance Act. What controls will be instituted to prevent fishing expeditions on the part of curious or vindictive administrators? How far will this administration go? These are serious questions which Members must ask themselves. How far wilT we allow "big brother" to go?
1 could go on. There are many other parts of this tax Bill which are clearly wrong-the treatment of automobile expenses, allowances for those living in our northern communities, retiring allowances, iron ore processing changes, and the elimination of the lower withholding tax on dividends from Canadian-controlled companies. That is a puzzler for me, from a Governement so intent on improving the degree of Canadian ownership. Through this Bill it takes away one of the incentives for increasing Canadian ownership.
Income Tax
I am sure my colleagues will raise these matters later in the debate. It is absolutely clear that there are sufficient reasons the Bill should not be passed. During the course of debate we will be putting up amendments on all these areas to try to improve the Bill and meet the objectives which we feel should be sought in a Bill such as this. If those amendments are not accepted, then we have no alternative but to vote against the Bill.
I say this because it undermines the strength of our small business community today, the source of some two-thirds of the jobs in the country. It undermines the ability of Canadians to prepare for retirement without fear of becoming overly reliant on Government. It also attacks the long-standing provision of confidentiality in the tax laws. It is against this background that the Minister is asking the House to ram the Bill through. As I said earlier, the Government House Leader wants the Bill passed in eight sitting days, by December 22. That is totally irresponsible. Let us not forget that it is basically the same bureaucrats who gave us the disaster of November 12, 1981 who also produced this Bill. There are 295 pages of very complex legislation, and the Government is asking us to give rubber stamp approval of it over the next eight days without proper debate. That is totally irresponsible.

Many Canadians have asked me personally to make sure that this Bill would be a good piece of legislation. They have kept after me with requests for amendments. This Bill is the most complex piece of tax legislation since the Benson reform 11 years ago. To pass this legislation in its entirety in eight days is both preposterous and unacceptable, as I see it.

The Minister says we need the legislation passed, that we need it to relieve Canadians of some uncertainty. I have been advised by lawyers and tax accountants that they do not need this legislation before mid-February next year. They are more concerned that the Government do it right this time and remove the worst parts of the Bill. If the Minister felt so strongly about getting this legislation through, why did he not bring it in at the end of October when it was ready? Or why did the previous Minister not bring it in last June when there was a detailed ways and means motion which proved that detailed tax legislation had been prepared? Why the delay? Why put Members of Parliament under the gun to try to pass this Bill in eight days?
It must be totally transparent by now that the only reason for the haste in rushing the Bill through the House in eight days is its fear of reopening the old wounds from November of last year. Sure, people want to know the rules of the game, but they also want to get the right rules of the game. That is the responsibility which Parliament has today.
If we needed any more proof of the transparent nature of the Government's pleas to get the Bill through, we have only to look at the red herring which the Minister and the Minister of
