December 13, 1982
Income Tax
State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove) have thrown out, saying that Canadians need tax refunds. These tax refunds will not be processed until the first of March anyway, so why the rush? Surely people understand that.
Returning to the budget of last November, it caused the most adverse and widespread reaction to Government policy that any of us in the House can recall. Our Conservative special committee on the budget experienced that first-hand when it travelled across the country. All Members of the House of Commons have received a massive response from their ridings, particularly at personal meetings and town-hall type meetings, as well as in letters. The former Minister of Finance had to take on a new staff of some 40 people just to answer his budget-related mail. It is human nature that the Government would want to avoid a repeat of that; we can understand that. But Members of Parliament have a greater responsibility to those Canadians affected than they do to the feelings of the present or former Minister of Finance. The Conservative Party is determined to give this legislation the responsible, comprehensive consideration and treatment which all Canadians expect from the House.
Before I close I want to ask Members and all Canadians to assess the Bill in the context of recent statements made by the Minister of Finance. He has said that there is not much that can be done, that the Government has done about all it can about the recession and that now it is up to the private sector to get the economy rolling again. How will the private sector do it? There are many remaining obstacles which will prevent the private sector from doing the job. 1 have spoken on many occasions about the vicious circle that we are in. Business activity is slow. Investment in new plant and equipment is projected to decline next year by 8 per cent. In 1982 it has already gone down signficantly. Business is not investing because consumers are not buying, and consumers are not buying particularly because they fear that they or someone in their families will lose their job. As I said, it is a vicious circle.
The key to breaking that vicious circle is to stabilize the unemployment outlook, to get business activity going and thereby increase the number of jobs available to Canadians. If we do not have this stability, which Canadians will buy new cars, stoves or houses, if they may need the money in a few months' time when they are laid off? This would give individual Canadians more confidence in the future, and only then would they consider making some of the purchases they have been putting off for such a long time.
The economic policy of the Progressive Conservative Party is aimed directly at breaking that log jam or vicious circle. How can we get business to hire more people? Existing companies are not likely to do this. They have been going through the wringer lately, cutting down the size of their operations. They have made many wrenching decisions to improve their productivity. Now we have to look elsewhere. We have to look outside the existing job-creation mechanism for new jobs.
Our economic policy has targeted five ways of encouraging new job-creating investment. The first is mini-projects, encouraging the start-ups of small businesses, encouraging
people to leave the comfort and security of well-paying jobs with large companies or Government. This is where this Bill is so wrong. In nine separate ways it makes it more difficult and less attractive for small business to prosper. It is more difficult for a person to leave that secure job, pull up stakes and build his future around the risky success of a small business. Many small-businessmen have told me that they would not leave a secure job with a large company today to start a small business. That attitude must be reversed if we are to create new jobs. The first steps toward changing that attitude can be taken by cancelling some elements of this Bill.
The Progressive Conservative economic policy would go further. We would take as a priority, as a new government, the objective of introducing a clear bias toward encouraging risktaking investment. This would provide a major step to improving our economic future.
Our second step is in the mega-projects. We would change those parts of the energy program which inhibit start-ups of these projects, the major sources of new job-creating investment. These changes would include the cancellation of the 25 per cent confiscatory back-in provision. They would also include a reduction in federal taxes where a reduction would contribute to major capital investment, such as in petrochemical projects where the federal natural gas tax has made these projects uncompetitive.
A third area of incremental investment is foreign investment. Foreign investment was actively discouraged by the former Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. This Government has acknowledged and has made some tentative changes in the operations of FIRA. More changes must be made to show that foreign investment is welcome in Canada, because it is investment that will create new jobs. It is investment incremental to that which we have in the country today.
As a fourth step we would reduce interest rates further. The inflation rate in the marketplace, the non-Government controlled part of the economy, is between 5 per cent and 6 per cent. The current interest rate at 13 per cent or 14 per cent is simply too high. It is a major deterrent to these new projects.
The fifth area that the Progressive Conservative policy would attack directly is the burden of Government. The current deficit of $24 billion is a dead-weight deficit. It is producing little by way of long-term job creation. Its size is both a psychological and a real burden on the capital market. It is inhibiting the reduction of interest rates.
Our policy would involve a reduction in Government spending. I have already touched on ways in which we would do that. Our policy would also involve a reduction in Government regulation and centralized decision making. Let me remind you again, Mr. Speaker, of the precise example I gave concerning income averaging annuities which took that decisionmaking process from the private sector and dropped it right into the middle of Government Departments. This is one area
December 13, 1982

we would reverse and one which would clearly address that problem.
It must be clear to Hon. Members that these five targets of Progressive Conservative economic policy would reduce the roadblocks to growth of which I have spoken. If these roadblocks are now removed, the private sector simply will not be able to do the job which the Minister is asking of it. All that the Government has offered is the six and five program. There is no long-term program. There is no program to remove these roadblocks to growth, so essential to the private sector being able to create jobs. I expect that the next budget in February or March next year will appear to go in that direction. It will sound pro-business, it will use the right words, but it will do nothing to change the direction which this Government has taken since 1980.
Let me point out two recent statements to support my thinking. The first is by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). Last week the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) asked why the Government had backed off on its stated intention to make the Foreign Investment Review Agency a more interventionist part of Government policy. Did the Prime Minister say his Government realized what it was proposing was wrong, that it would have been too interventionist, that the Government thought it might scare away foreign investment from the country? No, not at all. Not a word of withdrawal, nothing like that. The Prime Minister said only that there would be no changes because the economy today is too weak. What happens when the economy gets stronger? What does the threat of a stronger Foreign Investment Review Agency do to those contemplating investment in Canada today? It scares them away.
The second statement to support my thinking was by the Minister of Finance, to which I have referred.
Would you withdraw FIRA?

In answer to the Hon. Member, we would not do away with FIRA. We have proposed a number of specific changes in the Foreign Investment Review Agency to make it more effective in doing what it is supposed to do. Instead of being a policing agency as it is now, it would be a screening agency to get the right sort, the right type of foreign investment which will create the jobs and technology we need in Canada today and not scare that investment away.
We would make it a positive tool, not a negative one.

Let me refer again to the Minister of Finance's statement, to which I referred a moment or so ago. He said:
Now is not the time for further tax reform. The economy is too weak.
Again the Minister of Finance will wait until the economy recovers and then bring back those parts of the November budget that were dropped. The expectation that two of the greatest mistakes in the life of this Government will be repeated when the economy recovers will further slow down the economic recovery we need so much. Those two statements are
Adjournment Motion
very revealing of the way these two men think. Their action through this tax bill further supports my opinion.
My point, Mr. Speaker, is that I expect the policy of this Government to appear to be pro-business, and to be supportive of the private sector over the next few months. Then, because the road blocks are still there, job-creation and economic growth in the private sector will probably not be that good. The state will have been set. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance will be able to say: "We gave the private sector a chance; it did not perform. It dropped the ball. Now we will do it our way, by more intervention, more Government ownership and a higher Government deficit.''
What are the signs of that now? What makes me think that I am right when I make those statements? First, the Canada Development Investment Corporation has been created. There is no clear mandate for it. There is no parliamentary debate on what it will be doing. Those in charge are clearly identified with the more interventionist side of the Government. Senator Jack Austin, Maurice Strong and Joel Bell, the architects of the greatest thrust into the Canadian private sector that we have seen in years.
The Minister of Finance is already talking about possibly softening his stand on the size of the federal Government deficit. He has said: "Interest rates are coming down. Canadians seem to support a higher deficit. They are putting up billions to buy our Canada Savings Bonds." What a shortsighted point of view, but clearly one which is massaging public opinion in support of a larger deficit, a deficit which ultimately means higher taxes and more government in our lives.
In summary, this tax bill is the first sign of the Government's strategy to take a greater share of the economy. It confirms the Minister's words that he is prepared to rely more on the private sector, but these are only words. There is no evident desire to change the Government's fundamental course. The reduction in the capital cost allowance remains. The small business community remains under attack. Retirement savings are undermined.
We must defeat this Bill. We must work hard to change the damaging parts of the Bill. If we are not successful, I am sure that when we look back a year from now the direction toward greater Government control in our lives and the unhealthy private sector which must result from that will be abundantly clear. That is the mission on which we are embarked today.

speechtext:
Order, please. Before I recognize the next Hon. Member, may I deal with the debate on the adjournment motion this evening.

December 13, 1982
Income Tax
It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 40, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen)-Administration of Justice, (a) Mandatory supervision program-Release of dangerous sexual offenders, (b) Request for definition of "a bad evaluation"; the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan)-Administration of Justice-(a) Request for federal-provincial co-operation on issue, (b) Request that Minister take action; the Hon. Member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn)-National Security-(a) Case of Canadian professor-Application of Official Secrets Act. (b) Timing of decision of prosecution in Great Britain.
The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-139, to amend the Statute Law relating to Income Tax (No. 2) be read the second time and referred to a Committee of the Whole.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise to participate in the opening debate on Bill C-139, an Act to amend the statute law relating to income tax. I suspect that it should read "an Act to tinker with the statute law relating to income tax". This is a Bill consisting of 295 pages which has come about 13 months after the introduction of the budget of November 12, 1981. This Bill also brings into effect certain aspects of the June 28, 1982 budget, the mini-budget of October 27, 1982, as well as incorporating the material which was covered in 17 press releases by both the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and his predecessor.
The Minister of Finance is now asking us to jam this legislation through the House very quickly in the remaining eight days of this session. This Bill is 295 pages of very difficult, conflicting and confusing tax law. In effect, the Minister is asking us to have faith in his Government and ram this contract between the Government of Canada and the people of Canada through without bothering to read, study or debate it. I guarantee you, Mr. Speaker, that that is not what we intend to do. We do not plan to rush a document through the House when it affects every person in this country, especially when those effects are not beneficial.
In his most recent press conference, the Minister urged Parliament to end this time of uncertainty that surrounds the tax situation which has arisen from the last two and a half budgets. If the Minister of Finance expects this Bill to end the uncertainty in this country for one moment, I suspect that he must be a colleague of ET, someone coming from a different
planet. This Bill will not end uncertainty; it will add to uncertainty and confusion in terms of what lies ahead for the people of Canada.
1 clipped an interesting cartoon out of a newspaper from my constituency. It is an illustration of Mr. Hugh Hambleton's lawyer who is saying: "I respectfully submit, my Lord, that my client, Mr. Hugh Hambleton, passed some information to the Russians. But I can prove that he was a western agent working toward destabilizing the Soviet Union. The documents, my Lord, that he passed were blueprints of the Canadian Liberal Government's economic policy and tax laws." If anything was to destabilize an economy, it certainly would be the economic policies of this Government, complemented with its most recent introduction of tax reform.
This tax Bill comes before us at a time when there is a general sense of fear among Canadians across the country. Shortly after the introduction of the November 12 budget, the New Democratic Party toured the country with a series of open hearings in various towns. We asked for people's reactions to the budget. Whether the hearing was in eastern Canada, central Canada or western Canada, people demonstrated the same concern about the budget being a serious departure from traditional Government policy. There was very little in the budget to enhance the economic recovery which the country needed at that time. When we see the tax Bill that eventually evolved from the November budget and subsequent budgets, we find 13 months later a tax system that can only be described as a jungle. It is a tangle of legislation, regulations and interpretations that are becoming more entangled every year. The tax laws are virtually incomprehensible to almost everyone, including those in the tax Department.
As a matter of fact, the Minister of Finance was recently asked during a Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs hearing whether he could fill out his own income tax form. I give the Minister credit for honestly admitting that he found it impossible to fill out his personal income tax form; he had to go to a tax accountant for assistance. Here we have the Minister of Finance of Canada saying that he is unable to fill out a so-called simple tax form.
The small business sector is equally perplexed. I suspect that many small businesses are virtually on the edge of giving up totally. When one looks at the tax return that a small business is required to fill out and sees the pages of complex information that is required, one can see why a typical small business in this country literally throws these documents out of the door. These small businesses simply cannot handle the red tape, regulations and the jungle of information that they are required to give. They can no longer keep up with the requirements. Canadians are being asked today to participate in a tax process that is beyond comprehension. One simply has to call the tax Department and seek clarification or interpretation of what has been introduced in the last two and a half budgets in order to have an indication of the confusion in the Canadian tax system.
December 13, 1982

The Income Tax Act in 1971 consisted of approximately 916 pages of legislation. The Government has been attempting to streamline this legislation over the years in order to make it more simplified. However, when one compares the 1981 Income Tax Act to the 1971 Income Tax Act, one sees that it consists of 1,256 pages instead of the former 916 pages. In other words, the Government has added another third to the explanations in order to make it more understandable. This is the Government's notion of encouraging the private sector to participate in the system, but adding more and more pages of complex legislation seems to be a rather peculiar way to streamline the system.
As we move toward the end of 1982, the prevalent trend which we see today is for accountants to run around with their pocket calculators advising their clients about the various year-end tax plans. We see many advertisements at this time of year by the financial institutions which are encouraging people to buy RRSPs, RHOSPs, MURBs and participate in oil and gas and drilling funds. People are being encouraged to buy a share in a Canadian film. One begins to wonder what is happening. For whom are these tax deferrals designed? Are the textile workers and fishermen running out to participate in drilling funds? Are the IWA members or auto workers running out and picking up MURBs, or are the fellows down in the shops or the secretaries in the offices running out and selling off their stocks in order to get the $2,000 capital loss against other income?
Are tax deductions good or bad? A few months ago, MURBs were considered a good investment. The Government encouraged people to buy MURBs. We now find out that they are bad and people can no longer buy them. At one time the Government said that health and dental plans were beneficial and should be encouraged. It then said that these plans were bad and were to be taxed. Now it is again saying that they are good. The Government was saying that investment should be encouraged to buy stocks and the interest on that investment should be tax deductible. That was good then, but a few months ago we were told that it was bad and now, once again, we are told that it is good.
We were told that workers should be encouraged to move out into remote areas of the country to participate in resource development and that they should be encouraged to move there by having their housing subsidized. Then the former Minister of Finance suggested that that was a bad thing, and now we are hearing, once again, that it is not too bad, that it is only bad in certain instances but not in others. Is it any wonder that there is an incredible atmosphere of uncertainty and confusion when it comes to trying to figure out just what on earth the Government is trying to do?
We have heard Hon. Members discussing the whole matter of economic development and how it needs to be encouraged. We found out today that capital investment in this country will fall by $2.4 billion which, of course, will result in something
Income Tax
like an extra 280,000 jobs lost in 1983, plus many more unemployed as a result of the lack of consumer confidence.
The Government brings in legislation to kill economic activity, and it does it instantly. When one introduces tax legislation to stop a certain economic activity, it does it instantly. Then when one brings in tax reform to encourage certain kinds of investment, it takes place very slowly. It is a little like a marathon runner, running down the lane, and one walks up to him with a sledgehammer and busts one of his knees; it stops him dead in his tracks. Then we say: "We will just get that cast on and get him going again", but he moves off, very, very slowly.
The people of Canada have lost faith in this tax system. People have looked at the tax system and tried to figure out the motive behind it. Of course, one of the motives was that it would redistribute income in this country, yet when one looks at how income is distributed in Canada, comparing 1960 to 1980, one finds that the top small percentage still controls the majority of income and the percentage of poor remains the same. In other words, the rich are still in place and the poor are still in place, in the same percentages as they were 10 years, 20 years or 30 years ago. Therefore, in terms of redistribution of income, it has not happened.
We hear that the tax system is used by the Government to foster certain economic and social policies. While there has been marginal success in this area, it has been only marginal. I think one of the best examples of this was found in the incentive provided through the tax system for people to participate in the development of the Canadian film industry. With this incentive, upper income earners, by and large, were given a 100 per cent tax write-off if they bought shares in the Canadian feature film industry. In a sense, I think we must recognize that this is a direct grant to the upper income earners of this country to the tune of about $50 million a year. It is a hidden subsidy, then, to the upper income earners. However, the facts show that the films produced before this measure was introduced actually reflected the true essence of Canadian society better than those produced afterwards, because what kind of films were they? American movie moguls were coming into Canada, picking sites in Canada which would look very much like parts of San Francisco, New York, Wyoming or Alaska. There were also obvious, blatant tax avoidance efforts. There were certainly many stories going around concerning inflated movie budgets. In the end result, the movie industry in Canada was perhaps actually harmed as the result of this so-called tax incentive to encourage and invest in the film industry of this country.
In terms of using the tax system to advance good Government policy, that has not worked in Canada because so much of the policy has not been good. It has not been thought through in a careful way. That is why I was quite pleased when the Leader of my party suggested that, indeed, it was possible to use the tax system to encourage critical and strategic industries to develop programs in the research and development area, and to introduce affirmative action programs. In other words, to use the tax system to encourage and reward

December 13, 1982
Income Tax
those corporations which, in fact, were developing in the best interests, not only of themselves but of Canadians as well.
When one gets right down to it, one must admit that the tax system in this country has become nothing but a money grab, nothing but a revenue grab, nothing but a Government bailout, really, these days. It has created a very peculiar phenomenon in our country. A whole group of people have become participants in guerrilla warfare of tax avoidance. Tax evasion and tax avoidance are becoming almost a preoccupation with more and more Canadians. Normal, decent folks have been driven into discussing and planning how to avoid paying income tax in this country. Yes, 1 suspect that tax avoidance has moved from being a simple financial migraine into a financial epidemic in this country. If one goes into the bookstores at this time of year, one sees that the best sellers are those books telling one how to avoid paying income tax.
We can identify various groups, certainly those in the executive and highly paid professional category, who have the financial wherewithal to employ high-priced tax lawyers and accountants to assist them to dodge and weave through the various loopholes in the tax system. Then there are those upper middle class people who are exchanging services without any records to show financial transactions. For instance, someone will fix someone else's teeth in exchange for doing a tax return or will take on a particular legal case in exchange for the loan of a condominium in Maui. Goods and services are being exchanged with no record of transaction in terms of national revenue. This is occurring right on down to the blue collar workers, who are taking on extra jobs at night for cash at wages lower than what they would normally expect because the tax man will be unaware of such transactions. Someone will fix someone else's car in return for some plumbing work in the basement for that extra suite, and so on. An entire underground economy is developing, keeping money out of the federal treasury, affecting between 5 per cent and 20 per cent of our gross national product. It is a very serious situation when we have a system which is turning regular, normal, decent people into people who are trying to scheme and dodge around paying tax.
Why have people lost faith in the system? First, they have lost faith because they see how their money is being spent. After all, virtually every Canadian is affected by this tax system. Most Canadians are paying at least some income tax, particularly working Canadians. They see how it is being spent. It is almost like being spent by a drunken sailor but not quite, because a drunken sailor spends his own money. It is like being spent by a drunken sailor who is spending the petty cash he has lifted off the ship.
The Canadian people say that they are simply not appreciative of the way the Government is expending their money. Then when they consider how it is collected, they feel the tax system is obviously unfair and unjust. It favours certain income earners at the expense of others. To be very blatant about it, it favours the upper income people, the rich in this country. The budgets which have been introduced, in spite of what Ministers of Finance have said about their being more
equitable, more just, or more fair, have been quite the contrary.
The publication of one of the tax experts in this country is entitled "The New Canadian Tax and Investment Guide". This man has spent his entire life trying to advise people and finding ways to avoid paying tax, legally, as per the Income Tax Act. He says that the wealthy investor in Canada in 1983 will pay the same tax rate, even if his investment increases from, say, $200,000 to $300,000 in a given year.
While the MacEachen budget has been promoted as an attack against the rich, a close analysis of these numbers will show that the rich are virtually unaffected. For the rich and the super-rich the budget provides a 10 per cent decrease in tax rate.
One could look at what happens to one of these upper income earners in the Province of British Columbia or Ontario, just to take two Provinces as a sample. In 1981, under the old Budget, at a $100,000 income he would pay $32,589 in federal income tax. In 1982, as a result of the changes he would pay $29,085. When one considers that the provincial tax is related to the federal tax, for the person making $100,000 in British Columbia or Ontario, this budget and this tax Bill will save him in excess of $5,000 a year. Those are the facts.
What we are saying is that the tax system of this country favours certainly a very select upper income group, and that is why people are fed up. That is why people are going out of their way to try to find ways and means to manipulate the system to avoid paying what they know is an unjust tax.
Mr. Speaker, if you look very closely at the tax Bill and at the tax laws of this country, it becomes more incredible all the time: a tax system that consciously taxes the very poorest, those with incomes well below the poverty line. I raise this as a fundamental criticism of our tax system and one that really demonstrates clearly how desperate this Government is in terms of grabbing money.
In our country, the poverty level for a single person is about $5,000 a year. In 1981, a single person paying tax would have a number of deductions totalling something in the neighbourhood of $3,500. After $3,500, that single individual would be paying tax on money earned. What that says is that people who are living below the poverty line in this country, and there are hundreds of thousands of them in that category, are paying federal income tax. Surely to goodness we could allow an individual to work his or her way up to the basic poverty level of Canada before we start taxing them. But no, this Government taxes people whose incomes are below, and in many cases well below, the poverty line as defined by Statistics Canada. I think that demonstrates clearly just how desperate or perhaps how thoughtless this Government's tax system really is.
It gives millionaires a break.

It gives millionaires a break, as my colleague from Brant indicates.
December 13, 1982

Let us look at a few sectors of this tax Bill and how it impacts on certain sectors. Many of my colleagues in the days ahead will discuss the impact on the life insurance business, on the energy sector, on the agricultural sector, as it affects a number of women's issues, how it relates to the housing industry and how labour is influenced by this tax Bill.
1 want to just focus for a moment or two on the area of small business. I choose small business because this Bill, C-139, goes out of its way to make life miserable for the small business person. Here is a sector of our country made up of about 940,000 small businesses and shrinking, by the way, every day.
There is a story circulating as to how you start a small business in this country. The best way to build a small business or to find yourself the proprietor of a small business is to buy a large corporation, vote Liberal and wait a little while. Then, of course, you will end up with a small business very, very quickly.
These are the businesses that are virtually 100 per cent Canadian-owned. They are community oriented. They are labour-intensive as opposed to being capital-intensive. They represent the sector that is most effective in job creation. They do not send out vast amounts of money out of Canada in terms of interest and dividends. In other words, this is the sector of our economy that should be encouraged, that should be supported, that should be nurtured.
When you look at Bill C-139, you find that the Income Tax Act as it existed prior to the November budget-without taking into account Bill C-139-provided that a Canadian-controlled private corporation in the business of earning income from an active or non-qualifying business would be eligible for the low rate of 25 per cent, including provincial and federal combined tax; 25 per cent of the first $150,000 of income each year. When the small business has claimed the low rate on $750,000 during its lifetime, the small business would no longer be eligible for this low rate of tax and their tax rate would jump to the 50 per cent range.
However, if a corporation paid a taxable dividend to its shareholders, the payment of the dividend would then reduce the amount on which the low rate has been claimed. Thus, the shareholders of the small business corporation would make sure that the small business cumulative deduction account was rejuvenated by paying taxable dividends to himself or herself, or to the shareholders of that small operation. Then the individual would personally pay the tax on the taxable dividend, after the dividend tax credit.
What this meant was that the payment of the dividend rejuvenated the availability of the small business deduction in the year that followed. This provision enabled the small business peson to finance that operation from its earnings because of the shareholders reinvesting most of the dividends back into the small business. In other words, it enabled the small business to build equity capital, and it gave some encouragement for that small business to avoid going to the financial institutions and borrowing at excessive interest rates.
Income Tax
However, Bill C-139 changes all this, Mr. Speaker, the annual income eligible for the low tax rate will increase from the original $150,000 up to $200,000, and the total amount on which a corporation can claim the low tax rate, during the life of the corporation, is on accumulated earnings of $1 million as opposed to $750,000.
However-and this is where the major change has occurred-any dividends paid after 1981 will not rejuvenate the accumulated earnings account. Furthermore, the corporation may have already accumulated earnings of, say, $400,000 as a result of earnings in the past which have not been divi-dended out. If this corporation earns $200,000 in each of the next three years, it will run out of the $1 million limit and in year four, and from then on, it will no longer be eligible for the small business tax rate. On the other hand, a similar business which had been paying out dividends will have five years at $200,000 a year before it would end up paying the high tax rate of 50 per cent.
The question 1 want to put to Members opposite is, why do they think that a small business should be entitled to a low tax rate on only its first $1 million of accumulated earnings? Does that small business all of a sudden become a large business in the sixth year of its operation? The Act, in Section 72(c), which concerns the transfer of shares of small business corporations from a father to his children, provides that a small business corporation would be a Canadian-controlled private company which carries on an act of business. One has to wonder why this defined small business is not a small business at the end of five years, with accumulated earnings of $1 million. Do Members opposite intend to destroy the small businesses of Canada by asking them to pay at a high corporate rate, when in fact their economic situation remains totally unchanged?
One could also comment on the corporate distribution tax of 12.5 per cent, now that it has been levied on the small business. Of course, the result of this will be to encourage small business, rather than to continue on as a family operation, to sell up, so that the father who wants to sell to his son or to his daughter now will have to pay that 12.5 per cent. That will be encouragement to sell the operation lock, stock and barrel to someone else. Consequently we will see small business moving more and more into the national and multinational sector.
Let us be honest. This Bill was written for the large corporate sector and for the wealthy of Canada. It will make rich people richer and favour the rich at the expense of the poorer people of Canada. That is not rhetoric. Let us look at some of the facts.
Those with taxable income over $24,464 will receive a reduced tax rate as a result of this Bill. Those in the upper income levels with a taxable income of over $133,000 will have a significant tax decrease, from 43 per cent to 34 per cent. There will be a 9 per cent drop in the tax rate. This will result in a tax saving to the upper income earners per year of about

December 13, 1982
Income Tax
$5.7 billion, a nice subsidy for the upper income earners of Canada.
The 1978 tax returns indicated that well over 2,000 individuals who had assessed incomes of more than $50,000 paid no income tax at all. Hundreds who earned in excess of $100,000 paid no income tax. In 1979 more than $30 billion in revenues were lost to the Government as a result of tax loopholes.
While most Canadians were paying tax rates in the area of 20 to 25 per cent, the banks of Canada were paying a tax rate of 18 per cent, Power Corporation a rate of 11 per cent, the Steel Company of Canada 7 per cent, and Cadillac-Fairview 6 per cent. In other words, while the average working Canadian was being asked to pay 20 to 25 per cent of his income in tax, the banks and major real estate corporations were being asked to pay significantly less. When you look carefully at this Bill and the tax system, it is interesting to find that it is a kind of hidden subsidy or welfare for the upper earners of Canada.
In 1979 the Clark Government published the first Government report outlining the tax expenditure account. It proved beyond any question that most Government spending is actually done through the tax system, not through the usual kind of system such as DREE. In fact, eight times as much money was spent on housing and urban renewal through the tax system than through direct spending.
In the resource sector, the manufacturing sector, the general business incentive sector, the Government spent about $1.5 billion directly and about $6 billion through the tax system. As an example, take the income from capital gains. In 1978 1 per cent of tax filers accounted for 55 per cent of all the capital gain reported. Five hundred individuals with incomes over $100,000 recorded all their income from capital gains. A capital gain is only taxed half. In other words, half the capital gain is taxed. Another way of putting it is this. In 1980, $1 billion was spent to subsidize those who speculate in the securities and commodity markets and those who realize profit from real estate and other capital property sales.
This is justified by saying these people are in a high-risk area. They are risking their funds, but capital gains applies to all or any property. While it may be true in certain areas, it certainly would not be true for those who are making their capital gains through investment-induced stocks where the risk is indeed extremely minimal.
Over the last number of months, many people to my right have been railing on how they despise the way the Government spends on the CBC, and yet are quite willing to accept a 100 per cent tax break for those individuals invited to participate in the Canadian film industry.
Who can argue against charities? Let us look at who participates in contributions to charities. If you are in the $100,000 a year bracket, a $100 donation will cost you $39. If you are in the $10,000 a year bracket, a $100 donation to a charity fund will cost you $73. In other words, the tax system of Canada gives the wealthy much more power over the spending of Government money. One per cent of the taxpayers allocate about 35 per cent of all the Government funds that go to certain charities. The charities that are associated with and
encouraged by the upper income earners are the ones that are funded. Lower income Canadians do not have the same flexibility in the tax system to support the charitable organizations that they would like to support.
Let us deal with child care costs. We recognize today that with the state of the economy, it is important often for both parents to be away from home working. If a single parent is working, day care expenses become very important. If you are in the 65 per cent tax bracket, you get a subsidy from the Government of $650 for child care costs. If you are in the typical 20 to 25 per cent bracket, you get $250. If you are in the low income bracket you get nothing because there is no deduction. Any deduction in a low income area would be worthless. The Minister of Finance should say that we have a system which supports child care costs and some help to those who are very wealthy, a little less for the middle income group and nothing for the poor of Canada in terms of child care costs.
I listened with interest this afternoon when we were talking about deferred profit sharing. The idea behind that is good. However, when we hear that 90 per cent of the deferred profit sharing programs are used by firms participating with only three or fewer, we get the impression that this tax legislation is not being used for the purpose for which it was intended.
This Bill is simply too important and complex to gloss over. It is too important to pass quickly. In fact, when you consider what this Bill does, Mr. Speaker, it must be opposed. We waited 13 months for this Bill to come before the House. We know that there will be another budget in 90 days. There will likely be another set of tax changes. In the best interests of stability and certainty, perhaps we should hold off passing this Bill. Perhaps we should pass one Bill associated with that new budget and settle this whole matter. It would give the people of Canada some years where they could predict that no serious changes would be made to the tax laws.	.
I said at the outset of my comments that this Bill is tinkering with a system that is unjust. Further tinkering will not help the situation. When you consider the complexity, it is likely going to make it more unjust and more confusing. The average wage earners in Canada who cannot afford a tax lawyer or accountant to help them with their tax returns are being disadvantaged as the complexity grows more and more.
We plan to study this Bill very carefully. We plan to debate this Bill and point out its shortcomings in the hope that the Government will see fit to remove some of the more problematic clauses. We certainly do not plan to support this Bill so as to see its rapid completion in the next eight days before Christmas.

Mr. Speaker, it was almost exactly one year ago when I rose to speak on the origins of this income tax legislation, the November, 1981, budget. It has taken this Government 389 days to bring in the income tax
December 13, 1982

legislation to implement portions of that budget in the form of Bill C-139. This Bill is being presented by the new Finance Minister (Mr. Lalonde), a new hand at the helm of the financial ship of state, but these changes must be viewed in the context of the economic distress which this Government's fiscal and monetary policy has imposed on Canadians because we want to ensure that the measures in this Bill help to alleviate that stress.
A year ago I detailed the hardship, uncertainty and chaos being created by that November budget. 1 reviewed some of its most damaging aspects such as the taxation of income from life insurance, the removal of incentives for construction of rental accommodation, the blows to investment, the taxation of income before it is received and the taxation of employee benefits. I said then, that these measures are damaging at any time but are particularly destructive when the economy is in a tailspin. I quoted comments which I received from Canadians who are outraged by the ineptness and incompetence of this Government. And I concluded that speech by saying, "Canadians will not accept the budget. It has caused too much pain and too many broken commitments." It gives me no pleasure at all, Mr. Speaker, to look back at that time and realize that my comments were all too accurate. That budget has had a devastating impact on the economy, on business, on investors, and on Canadians in general.
My Province of British Columbia has been particularly hard hit this year both by the recession and by this Government's policies. Its major employer, the forest sector, for example, is struggling to survive. We have heard in this House about the threat to our soft wood lumber exports which we face from the U.S. Major lumber companies are reporting huge third-quarter losses. For instance, one of our largest firms, MacMillan Bloedel Limited, of Vancouver has fired 22 per cent of its salaried work force, and at one point had laid off almost half of its hourly-paid employees. Fourth quarter losses are expected to be high also. The Council of Forest Industries reports between 25 per cent and 30 per cent of British Columbia lumber mill capacity is closed. The devaluation of the Scandinavian currency has had a stunning impact on our hopes for an early recovery of our offshore pulp markets. The IWA expects that total lay-offs will rise to 20 per cent of the lumber industry's work force. There are some towns, such as Port Alberni, which face 30 per cent to 40 per cent unemployment. Yet this Government has brought in no long-term solution to deal with some of these fundamental economic problems.
The hardest task to deal with, Mr. Speaker, for any Member of Parliament on either side of the House today is unemployment in his riding. We are daily meeting with very proud people, people in shock, people who have given the best years of their lives to agencies or to companies and who are out of work. Some of these people no longer even ask us to help them get jobs. Their problem is that they are running out of their unemployment insurance benefits and they are desperate for any measure at all that we can give them to re-enter the labour force. Given that reality in our ridings, I was truly astounded to hear the Finance Minister today say he expected unemployment to drop next year, because that is not the reality that we face here today. It is in keeping with this Government's track
Income Tax
record, however, of disastrous economic policies and poor forecasts.
While B.C.'s unemployment soared by 100 per cent this year over last, this Government was draining the investment needed to create jobs through a series of anti-investment measures. With mines closing throughout the Province, the Minister planned to tax employee benefits and northern allowances, thus making remote sites uneconomical. As the B.C. economy plunged, the Government proposed to make it harder for Canadians to provide for their future by taxing life insurance, restricting the $1,000 pension deduction and disallowing the deduction of interest costs on funds borrowed to invest in registered retirement savings plans and deferred profit-sharing plans. While the number of business bankruptcies in B.C. doubled this year, this Government was gutting the small business development bond, eliminating reserves and applying a 12.5 per cent tax on dividends.
For over a year now this Government has not addressed the central issue facing our country today, the collapse of the economy. In fact, its policies have been making our problems very much worse. In my riding of Vancouver Centre, for example, small independent retailers of high fashion footwear are being put out of business by the Government's import quotas on footwear. These quotas were imposed last summer to protect the jobs of Canadian manufacturers in Central Canada at the expense of jobs elsewhere. Unfortunately, the Canadians who are being put out of business are the small retailers who sell highly specialized shoes for which there is no Canadian manufacturer. One merchant in my riding, for example, sells shoes which are designed in Canada by Canadians, but made offshore because it is uneconomical for any Canadian manufacturer to produce them. The quota he was allocated is too small to keep him in business and, unfortunately, he received his quota two months after the deadline for appealing it had passed. He tells me that unless he is allocated sufficient quota to keep him in business, he must close his doors. This Government, therefore, is forcing Canadians out of work in order to protect jobs which do not exist and cannot exist because of the size of the market in this country.
As a result of the Government's economic policies, a great deal of damage has been caused, and some of it long-term. The loss of faith and confidence in the future which some of my colleagues have referred to, Canadians will feel for a long time to come. For instance, a woman wrote to the Finance Minister about her husband. She said:
My husband's UIC ran out in June. He has been looking for employment for over a year. I have watched this man, who has lots of ability and experience in many areas, a man who would be an asset to anyone who would employ him, become discouraged, disheartened and finally to begin to feel that he is of no value to anyone. Whatever you think may happen in the decade of the 80s will be likely too late for us, and there are thousands like us.
Canadians have also lost faith in their Government. I continually meet Canadians with years of professional service who are out of work. I remember meeting with one bureaucrat who said he deals with former colleagues of his, people he went

December 13, 1982
Income Tax
to college with, people he worked in business with, who are out of work, and their attitude toward him as a secure bureaucrat is one of burning resentment. Distrust, indifference and resentment are dangerous attitudes if we want to work together in the future to pull ourselves out of this crisis. As one of my constituents said in a letter:
I do not believe that the Canadian taxpayer will trust any Government incentive program for quite some time.
In fact, who could blame them? Businesses which have gone bankrupt will not easily re-open their doors. A senior citizen on a very limited income told me, "This budget is making everyone live in fear, and fear is foreign to me." She will not forget that feeling of insecurity. The tenants who cannot find affordable housing will never recapture the exorbitant rents they are having to pay because the Government removed effective incentives to build. Many Canadian taxpayers will pay more tax because the Government changed the taxation rules and disrupted their planning. Many Canadians will never return to their jobs because their jobs have vanished. And this is particularly hard on the young Canadians who tend to be the last hired and the first fired.
When 1 am working in my riding with Government programs which are too narrow to deal with the problems, one of the toughest problems 1 have is finding work for young kids who do not have a work record, do not have unemployment insurance and cannot qualify for the Government's job creation programs.
One of my constituents is a chartered accountant who wrote me recently that his practice had grown substantially for all the wrong reasons and he said his clients are desperate to find ways to survive while dealing with problems beyond their understanding. I think this constituent has touched on one of the major problems underlying this Government's economic policies, and that is the intrusion of the state into areas which have previously been reserved for the individual.
There are two disturbing themes which can be identified through the last two budgets, the Minister's economic statement, and in this income tax legislation. The first is the fact that the Government is forcing Canadians to depend on the state rather than on themselves. Second, the Government is taking money from people before they receive it. These two themes have formed the basis for the original November budget, and they are present in this income tax legislation.
There is no question, Mr. Speaker, but that this income tax legislation is a much improved document over that first budget. Over the last 13 months some 47 retreats and withdrawals have been made to the initial proposal, largely because of the efforts of the Official Opposition on behalf of and working with Canadians hurt by the budget. Certainly we welcome some positive measures that the Government has included in the legislation. I am glad to see, for example, that the Child Tax Credit has been increased by $50 per year, per child. 1 think this credit is one of the most fair means of helping out families with children. I applaud any move to strengthen it. With my NDP colleague, the Hon. Member for
Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), 1 would welcome any measure to extend daycare credits.
1 think our income tax legislation is improved by the provision in the Bill which permits the tax-free transfer of an RRSP between spouses in the event of a marriage breakup. That is a constructive move. I am also very pleased to see that the Government has agreed not to touch the employer contribution to health and dental plans. I was afraid that if this measure had been included in the legislation, many Canadians would simply opt out of these plans.
Today the Minister of Finance claimed that the legislation reduces taxes for 5.8 million Canadians, for a total saving of approximately $1 billion per year. What the Minister failed to acknowledge is that the major beneficiaries are high income Canadians whose marginal tax rates has been reduced. Low and middle income Canadians gain little or nothing from lower or marginal tax rates and will lose proportionately more from the partial deindexation of old age and public service pensions.
Many employees are also adversely affected by the 40 per cent increase in unemployment insurance premiums announced by the Minister in his October economic statement and by the increased taxation of some important employee benefits. As an example, loans to employees to permit them to purchase a home or shares in their company will become taxable. This measure discourages employees from investing in their own firms, which is a measure that we need in order to encourage the productivity increases that we need to fuel our recovery.
In the case of loans for housing, it also represents a real barrier to worker mobility. As the Council of Forest Industries of B.C. wrote me, this will make it even more difficult to attract employees to areas of high housing costs, such as outside Vancouver. This measure seems particularly ill-timed, since the federal Government has been strongly encouraging the Provinces to eliminate all barriers to worker mobility. The cost of housing is certainly a major barrier to that kind of mobility.
Similarly, the standby charge on which the amount of taxation on company cars is calculated has been doubled. We in the Official Opposition did succeed in persuading the Government to limit the increase, since the November budget proposed an even higher rate of taxation, and we are pleased that the Government has agreed to modify the taxation for those who do not use their cars a great deal for personal business. We still believe this is an unnecessary tax increase at a time when this industry has been hit very hard by the recession. Many auto dealerships across the country have gone bankrupt over the past year, and yet the Government persists in adding to their burden by forcing the employers and the employees to keep much more detailed records in order to exact this tax.
One of the meanest aspects of this Income Tax Act is its effect on Canadians who are retired or who are trying to provide for their retirement. Many of these changes are
December 13, 1982

extremely complicated and confusing to seniors who often do not understand the rules which keep changing and which are much more complex than they have been accustomed to.
For example, the Government has restricted the amounts that can be rolled over tax-free into registered pension plans and Registered Retirement Savings Plans, to $2,000 per year of employment plus $1,500 for each year that no money was contributed to a pension plan. Originally, the impact of this measure would have been extremely harsh, because it was retroactive. Many people who planned to retire at the end of 1981 were going to be affected without warning. For that reason, we forced the Government to grandfather this measure. Nevertheless, the Government severely disrupted the financial planning of many groups nearing retirement. We heard from many professional groups such as the Police Association of Ontario and the B.C. Federation of Teachers.
As one Canadian said of this measure in his letter to the Minister of Finance, "If the intent is to get people to not plan for retirement but rather to count on Guaranteed Income Supplements or other Government assistance, you are on the right track."
Furthermore, this Bill denies registration for future deferred profit sharing plans which allow an owner to qualify for a plan. It prevents owner-managers from using this means to provide for retirement. It is very unfair, particularly to small businessmen who may not know how much money their company will earn in a year and who draw limited salaries.
I was in that position when I ran my own company, before being elected. Everyone else is paid first, the bills are paid and then the boss is paid. A deferred profit sharing plan was a simple way to allocate part of your own wage cost when you did not know how much you would earn in a year. Its loss is going to be a very bad thing for a lot of small businessmen, particularly in times when costs are hard to forecast.
In addition, this legislation eliminates the deductibility of interest on loans taken out to purchase RRSPs. Particularly hard hit are middle-income Canadians since many rely on RRSPs to provide income security for their future. In fact, nearly 1 million people earning less than $30,000 per year declare contributions to RRSPs as deductions. Many of them borrow money to purchase their RRSPs because they do not happen to have the lump sum available to meet the purchasing deadline early in the year. This measure hurts low income Canadians. Fligher income people have the money available. As our task force toured the country it was told this by many groups, over and over again. As many of these loans are paid off within the year, they are a form of forced savings. In effect, the Government is penalizing Canadians for prudently putting money aside.
Another harmful measure in this legislation is the limits to the $1,000 pension deduction. In most cases the pension deduction is limited for those under age 60 who roll over a pension benefit into an RRSP. This affects those who retire early and who may wish to shelter income which at the present time is surplus to their needs. That is important in bad times when people are being asked to retire early. It also denies the
Income Tax
pension deduction to those who receive lumpsum pension benefits in any form other than life annuities.
As with so many of the Government's measures, it hits hardest those most vulnerable-those Canadians who are at the end of their salaried years and who face a future on a fixed income.
Many small businessmen, farmers and those who are employed in seasonal occupations such as fishing and logging, are particularly hard hit by the elimination of general averaging and income averaging annuity contracts and their replacement with forward averaging.
For those who receive a once-in-a-lifetime income which they would like to set aside for their retirement, the IAAC is no longer available. For those whose income varied with the seasons and the harvests, the automatic system under which their gains and losses were evened out by the tax system is no longer available.
Both systems have been replaced by a very complicated procedure called forward averaging, in which a taxpayer will have to estimate whether his income will fall in the coming years, prepay the tax at the top marginal tax rate and claim it back in the future. He will have to hire an accountant to pilot him through the extremely complicated procedures. Should he neglect to tell the Government he intends to forward average initially-either because he does not understand the system or because he does not realize his income in future years will fall-he will not be able to claim back the tax he has paid. He is taking all the risk while the Government has fully hedged its bets, taking the money. Those who suffer least are those in top tax brackets who lose nothing by electing to forward average since they have to pay the top rate anyway.
After attacking in so many ways the ability of older Canadians to provide for their retirement, the Government caps it off by limiting the indexing of old age pensions and Public Service pensions. Nearly 1.2 million Canadians are affected by these two measures which are enshrined in Bills C-131 and C-133 currently being studied by committees of the House. What these measures represent collectively is best described by two people who wrote me from Vancouver. One investment analyst said the following about the victims of these measures:
Probably not since the depression years of the 1930s has a group of Canadians suffered such drastic reversals in their economic fortunes while having paid comparatively high tax levels during their productive years and having no responsibility whatsoever for the economic plight they find themselves faced with today, to say nothing of the loss of personal pride and dignity.
Recently the Minister of Finance said that he expected older Canadians to shoulder their share of the battle against inflation. As the President of the Vancouver branch of the Federal Superannuates National Association said with reference to the deindexing of Public Service pensions:
These are the same Canadians that were obliged to carry the main burden of the 1930-1939 depression. A great number of these Canadians bear the psychological scars of unemployment during their youth; of living in family homes in which welfare payments were their main subsistence; of soup kitchens

December 13, 1982
Income Tax
and "riding the rods". This group of older Canadians is also the group that was called upon to carry their load during the period 1939-1945 war and facing all the rigors that war involves.
This group is one of the major victims of the Government's economic policies. They have suffered through a recession which has been made worse by a Government that is incompetent and shortsighted. They are being penalized for attempting to provide for themselves and for trusting the Government. The irony is that at the same time as the Government reduces the indexing on pensions, it is forcing more Canadians to become even more reliant on income from state resources after retirement.
In conclusion, I should like to touch briefly on the other very dangerous principle which underlies the Government's economic policies, that is, to tax money before it is received by the taxpayer. In his statement today, the Minister of Finance neglected to point out that that is still an underlying theme. The November budget established a very dangerous principle when it dwelt on the concept of tax expenditures and argued that the Government is forgoing a great deal of revenue by not imposing taxes on certain kinds of hidden income or imputed income.
The Government argued that many taxpayers were receiving benefits on which they were not paying tax, and it set out to capture some of this revenue. In the November budget, for example, it proposed to tax Canadians who sold property and then took back mortgages. Where in the past the taxpayer paid taxes as he received income, the Government proposed to force him to pay tax on the sale as if he or she received a lump sum from the purchaser rather than in instalments on a regular basis.
If we had not forced the Government to alter this provision, most small land developers would have been put out of business and with them the jobs they create would have disappeared. The Government has applied the same principle to the taxation of life insurance and annuities. Fortunately we have been successful in persuading the Government to modify the provision, but the principle remains and is embodied in this income tax legislation. Accrued income on some kinds of life insurance will now be taxable, thus affecting those Canadians for whom these policies are a major form of retirement income. Similarly, accrued interest on annuities is now taxable. Income from annuities is calculated every three years and tax must be paid on that amount even though the taxpayer does not receive a direct benefit from the annuity at that time. With the Government operating on this deemed-income principle, who knows what may become taxable in the future?
The income tax legislation before us requires careful scrutiny. It is extremely complicated. As the Minister of Finance said today in the House, income tax legislation is forbiddingly complex. This Bill is nearly 300 pages long. It has been pointed out that it is the most complex document we have seen since the Carter Commission on Taxation, a Commission which produced seven volumes of work, which met and held public hearings for months to discuss similar types of measures.
We in the Conservative Party have acted very responsibly in the past year in our efforts to gather information about the impacts of this income tax legislation, in our task force on the budget which travelled the country, in the volume of correspondence from constituents across the country with which we dealt, and in trying to seek, through committees, constructive solutions to some of the changes.
We are not about to be rushed now into forcing this legislation through the House. We are not here to stonewall the legislation, but we are here to ensure a sense of security about the measures contained in the legislation. It was this Government that created the tremendous uncertainty about our income tax legislation; trying to rush the legislation through will simply compound the problem. There are examples, for instance, in terms of work in progress. For many firms such as engineering and economic consulting firms, this measure will impose undue economic hardship.
I should like Government Members to consider the case of Dome Petroleum which hired all its consultants. The industry says that in the worst days of its financial difficulties it simply did not pay them. Is the Government proposing that those people bear the entire brunt of this kind of legislation?
We in the Conservative Party are anxious to proceed in a responsible manner with what we hope is the final instalment of this long budget process. We do not want to be identifying and debating once again unworkable aspects of the Bill long into the future. Stability is the key which we are seeking, and stability requires that we ensure that when this legislation is approved, it is the best we can make it.
Hear, hear!

It is fair to say that the provisions in the Bill touching on small businesses, which are mainly involved with amendments to Section 125 of the existing Income Tax Act, are nothing but a morass. Mr. Speaker, 1 must apologize for delaying the House. But as you know, we sometimes run into conflicts. Tonight there is a dinner meeting in the Railway Committee Room, which went a little longer than anticipated. In fact, the bells started to ring just as the main course was being brought in. I can only apologize in the sense that I was the unfortunate victim of the conflicts with which we live in the politics of Canada.
As you will recall, Mr. Speaker, I was simply pointing out that in sharp contrast to what the Minister of Finance had indicated as something that would remove uncertainty with respect to our tax laws and would, to use his words, "affect taxpayers and allow them to know precisely where they stand", that was really stretching the English language when one considers the type of Bill in the form of an amendment to the Income Tax Act that we have before us in Bill C-139.
I was reading in particular only parts of the Clause dealing with small business taxation. I pointed out that surely when you read the wording in that Clause, it is almost incomprehensible, certainly to us in the House of Commons and I would suggest even to the tax lawyers and accountants who are being asked to cope with these sections and passages every day of the week. This matter was brought to my attention soon after this Bill was tabled on December 7 by a number of tax authorities in Toronto and in other localities in Canada. After receiving the Bill and spending four hours reading the Clause, in the case of one of the largest chartered accountant firms in Canada, its experts were still unable to know how to advise their client as to the impact of the Clause.
If we could just follow the Clause to which I was referring starting on page 189, we find sub-paragraph 125(6)(6)(iii), of which I will read the preliminary part. It goes on to subparagraph (iii.l) where it states:
where the year in its first taxation year ending after 1982, the amount, if any, of the prescribed addition to the cumulative deduction account of the corporation, and
(iii.2) the aggregate of all amounts each of which is an amount required to be added to the amount of the cumulative deduction account of the corporation at the end of the year under subsection (8.1) or (8.4).
(5) Subparagraphs 125(6)(6)(iv) and (iv.l) of the said Act are repealed and the following substituted therefor:
I quote that just as an example. But this goes on not by the page or by tens of pages, but by hundreds of pages. We have a little less than 300 pages in this Bill that, if passed, will be put before the people of Canada, particularly those who have to pay taxes in this country, who will be asked to please pay up. It is "pay up the taxes" that in effect we say are properly payable under this Bill.
Let us put that into perspective. We are amending here an Income Tax Act that first began in 1917. It is interesting to look at the initial act. I have here a copy of the initial Act passed by this Parliament in 1917, at that time as a temporary war measure. The Act passed in 1917, was ten pages long; including the schedules it amounted to 11 pages. It had only 24 clauses, and that was it. Yet here a simple amendment to that
